strengths: Novel and creative reformulation of DNA sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding, departing from the dominant sequence-token paradigm and introducing region-centric primitives (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion) that are well-aligned with practical genomic operations such as variant localization and subsequence retrieval.

Strong and fairly broad empirical validation: consistent gains over multiple recent, competitive baselines (HyenaDNA, Caduceus-Ph, JanusDNA, Evo-2 7B, LucaOne 1.8B) across three qualitatively different benchmarks (long-range eQTL prediction, cross-subspecies OOD generalization, whole-genome phenotype prediction), suggesting the representation is not overfit to a single task type.

A well-isolated controlled ablation (Section 4.3, Q1) directly compares OpticalDNA against its own backbone (DeepSeek-OCR) under identical protocol, providing reasonably convincing evidence that the DNA-specific document formulation and pretraining tasks—not just the vision backbone itself—drive the improvements.

Extensive documentation of task design principles, prompt/response protocols, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics (Appendices A–I), which substantially aids reproducibility and transparency, including per-tissue breakdowns and additional per-task diagnostic metrics (T2–T6).

Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM) offering qualitative evidence that the model attends to biologically meaningful loci (donor splice sites), which is a meaningful complement to the accuracy-only evaluation and differentiates this work from black-box sequence models.

Efficiency analysis (Table 7) showing the compression ratio can be increased substantially with negligible accuracy loss, supporting the claimed favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for long genomic contexts.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claims (e.g., '20x fewer effective tokens', '985x fewer activated parameters') compare against base-level tokenization and full-parameter baselines rather than more competitive efficient tokenization schemes (e.g., k-mer or existing compressed genomic encoders), which may overstate the practical advantage; a more rigorous comparison against equally optimized sequence-based compression baselines is missing.

The controlled 1D-vs-2D CNN comparison in Appendix A uses weak, non-standard 1D CNN baselines (a custom family and a weak SimpleCNN) rather than strong sequence models (e.g., HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2) under the same compute/parameter budget, limiting the strength of the core motivating claim that 2D document-style processing is intrinsically superior to sequential reading.

For DNALONGBENCH, OpticalDNA uses a frozen huge backbone (multi-billion parameter visual encoder/decoder) with only a small trainable probe, while baselines like JanusDNA are trained end-to-end at much smaller total scale; the 'trainable parameter' and 'activated parameter' comparisons, while technically accurate, could be seen as an apples-to-oranges comparison that inflates the apparent efficiency advantage of OpticalDNA.

The rice whole-genome phenotype benchmark (RiceWGPB) is based on very small sample sizes (21–26 test examples for TGW/LRI), making the reported RMSE differences potentially unstable and not strongly statistically supported; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any benchmark.

The paper's core conceptual claim that DNA is 'sparse and discontinuous' and thus better suited to 2D spatial layouts is not fully substantiated: the rendering into rows/pages is an arbitrary raster-scan of the 1D sequence (line-wrapping is not biologically informed), so it is unclear that genuine long-range or discontinuous dependencies are converted into meaningful 2D spatial structure rather than an arbitrary re-chunking that happens to benefit from convolutional inductive biases.

Some evaluation results reveal notable limitations that are underexplored in the main text: chromosome classification (T6) achieves only 6–10% accuracy, and DNA subsequence localization (T5) shows steep accuracy degradation under stricter IoU thresholds, indicating the framework's grounding/retrieval capability is considerably weaker than its transcription capability; these weaknesses are relegated to the appendix rather than discussed prominently.

Reproducing baselines (Evo-2, LucaOne) via a custom feature-extraction and linear-probing pipeline (with truncated context windows, e.g., 70k for Evo-2 vs. the paper's own 400k+ inputs) may not reflect these models' true best-case performance, raising concerns about baseline fairness in the rice benchmarks.

The Grad-CAM interpretability analysis is based on only two qualitative examples without quantitative localization metrics (e.g., overlap with annotated splice sites averaged over a test set), so the interpretability claims remain largely anecdotal.

strengths: Creative reformulation of DNA modeling as OCR-style document understanding, building on a real VLM (DeepSeek-OCR) backbone rather than a toy architecture.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three benchmark suites (DNALONGBench eQTL, RiceSubBench OOD, RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype) with consistent gains over strong baselines (HyenaDNA, Caduceus, JanusDNA, Evo-2, LucaOne).
Thorough appendix documenting prompt protocols, rendering procedures, and hyperparameters, which aids reproducibility of the rendering/prompting pipeline.
Interesting efficiency result: compression ratio can be increased ~20x via higher rendering resolution with negligible AUROC change (Table 7), suggesting practical token-budget flexibility.
Ablation against the DeepSeek-OCR backbone isolates the effect of DNA-specific pretraining, showing measurable (if modest) gains.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claims (e.g., '985x fewer activated parameters,' '20x fewer effective tokens') are presented in a misleading way: the comparison counts only 'trainable' parameters (256K) while ignoring that the frozen/LoRA-adapted backbone used for feature extraction is itself a 3.4B-4B parameter vision-language model, which is far larger than the baselines being 'outperformed.' This is an apples-to-oranges framing of model efficiency.

Core OCR-style primitives that motivate the entire framework perform poorly in the paper's own appendix evaluations: T5 subsequence localization has Det-Acc as low as 0.0055-0.0623 at IoU=0.99, T4 masked completion Text-EM is only ~0.13 and degrades sharply with span length, and T6 chromosome classification accuracy is only 0.06-0.10. These results directly undercut the claimed 'close alignment' between OCR primitives (grounding, retrieval, completion) and genomic reasoning tasks highlighted as a key contribution.

The central motivating argument -- that genomic 'sparse, discontinuous, jump-like' semantics benefit from document/layout structure akin to OCR -- is not well supported mechanistically: the rendered 'DNA document' is literally uniform monospace text wrapped into fixed-width lines with no real heterogeneous layout (no headers, columns, or structural variation as in natural documents), so the OCR analogy is largely cosmetic rather than reflecting genuine spatial semantics.

The Appendix A motivating comparison (1D CNN vs. 2D CNN on eQTL) that anchors 'Limitation 1' is not a controlled test of the sparse/discontinuous-semantics hypothesis; it conflates architecture family, parameter count, and possible pretrained-weight advantages of TIMM 2D backbones vs. hand-built 1D CNNs, weakening the evidentiary basis for the paper's core motivation.

There is a substantial, unaddressed gap between the 2048-bp pretraining window (HG38) and the much longer downstream evaluation contexts (up to 450k bases, or ~400M bases for whole-genome phenotype prediction), with no ablation clarifying how/why representations trained on short windows generalize to such drastically longer sequences via simple multi-page mean pooling.

Baseline reproduction for Evo-2 and LucaOne uses naive fixed-length chunking plus mean pooling to extract features, which is a crude adaptation that likely handicaps these autoregressive long-context models and makes the 'OpticalDNA beats much larger models' claims less convincing.

Compute cost of pretraining (8 days + 3 days on 8xH100 for HG38; 5 days for rice) is substantial but not weighed against the 'efficiency' narrative; efficiency claims focus narrowly on inference-time token counts/trainable parameters while downplaying considerable pretraining cost.

Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM) is limited to two anecdotal case studies without quantitative validation against known functional annotations, making the interpretability claims largely qualitative and not rigorously substantiated.

Important weaknesses (T4/T5/T6 failures) are relegated to the appendix while the main text and abstract emphasize only favorable comparisons, giving an overly optimistic impression of overall primitive-level performance.

strengths: Original and creative reframing of genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding, departing from the dominant token-sequential paradigm used by nearly all prior DNA foundation models.

Extensive and carefully constructed experimental suite: three progressively harder benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, RiceSubBench cross-subspecies OOD, RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype prediction), plus a 1D-vs-2D CNN controlled ablation (Appendix A) motivating the core hypothesis.

Strong empirical results with substantial parameter/token efficiency: competitive or superior AUROC/accuracy versus HyenaDNA, Caduceus, JanusDNA, Evo-2 (7B) and LucaOne (1.8B), while tuning only 256K-2.3M parameters and using far fewer activated/trainable parameters.

Thorough reproducibility documentation: detailed rendering protocol, bounding-box construction, six prompt-family task definitions with exact response templates, training hyperparameters for both pretraining stages, and grid-search ranges for downstream tuning, provided across many appendix sections.

Thoughtful ablations isolating sub-capabilities (ROI grounding T2, ROI transcription T3, masked completion T4 with span-length stratification, subsequence retrieval T5, chromosome classification T6), which honestly reveal both strengths (near-perfect transcription robustness, strong line-level grounding) and clear weaknesses (poor T5 localization under strict IoU, weak T6 chromosome classification), reflecting an honest treatment of limitations.

Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM over multi-page fusion) provides a qualitative link between visual attribution and biologically annotated splice sites, adding some practical value beyond raw accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: The central analogy—that DNA rendered as monospace text has meaningful 'document layout' analogous to natural documents—is not well justified. Unlike real documents, the line-wrapping/page boundaries are purely artifacts of an arbitrary fixed canvas width and font size, not any biological spatial structure; it is unclear whether the model learns genuine 2D regularities or merely exploits a fixed-stride chunking equivalent to k-mer tokenization in disguise. The paper does not include a controlled comparison against strong k-mer/stride-based tokenization baselines at matched compression ratios to isolate whether gains come from 'vision/OCR' processing per se or simply from a different (larger) effective token granularity.

Baseline comparisons for Evo-2 (7B) and LucaOne (1.8B) use these models purely as frozen feature extractors with mean-pooled embeddings and a linear/shallow head (Appendix G.2), which may not reflect their intended or strongest usage mode (e.g., no fine-tuning, no architecture-specific scoring/embedding strategies); the reported accuracies for these large models look surprisingly weak (e.g., Evo-2 ~0.70 AUROC, near chance-level accuracy in Table 3), raising concerns about whether the comparison is fully fair rather than reflecting a fundamental advantage of OpticalDNA.

Total training cost for the proposed pipeline (8+3 days on 8×H100 for HG38, plus a separate ~5-day rice run, built atop a 3B/3.97B-parameter OCR backbone) is substantial and not directly compared in wall-clock/FLOPs terms against training lightweight sequence models (HyenaDNA, Caduceus) from scratch; the paper emphasizes downstream inference-time efficiency but is less transparent about total pretraining compute trade-offs.

Several component evaluations reveal weak absolute performance that undercuts the 'understanding-driven compression' narrative: subsequence localization (T5) achieves very low IoU-based detection accuracy under realistic thresholds, chromosome classification (T6) accuracy is only 6-10%, and masked completion (T4) exact-match drops sharply with span length—suggesting the model's claimed region-aware/global reasoning capabilities are quite limited in practice despite being central motivating primitives.

Downstream evaluation relies on frozen-encoder linear/MLP probing on relatively small, task-specific datasets (nine GTEx tissues, a handful of rice accessions, ~100-130 phenotype samples), which is a reasonable but narrow test of representation quality; no significance testing, variance across seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the main results tables, making it hard to assess the robustness of reported improvements, especially on the very small RiceWGPB dataset (26-21 test samples per trait).

The method has been validated on only two species (human and rice); generalization to genomes with different repeat structure, GC content, or without well-curated long-range annotation (needed to construct bounding boxes/labels) is untested, limiting claims of broad applicability.

The free-form DNA transcription (T1) 'OCR' task is in part a self-referential check of whether the model can reconstruct text it was itself shown to render, and the large accuracy gap versus the off-the-shelf DeepSeek-OCR backbone mainly demonstrates successful domain-specific fine-tuning on a narrow font/layout rather than a fundamentally new capability.

strengths: Creative and genuinely novel reformulation of genomic sequence modeling as an OCR-style document understanding problem, departing from the dominant sequence-token paradigm.

Extremely thorough empirical validation: results span three benchmark families (DNALONGBench eQTL, RiceSubBench cross-subspecies OOD, RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype), with consistent gains over strong baselines (JanusDNA, NT-v2, GENERator, Evo-2, LucaOne) while using far fewer trainable/activated parameters and tokens.

Unusually extensive and transparent appendix material covering contamination analysis (strict full-sequence overlap and k-mer containment studies to rule out memorization), rendering/formatting robustness, low-resolution robustness, token-bottleneck ablations, cross-species transfer controls, and detailed reproducibility documentation (prompt templates, conversation schema, hyperparameters) — this substantially strengthens confidence in the reported numbers and reproducibility.

Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM on multi-page fusion) provides qualitative evidence that the model attends to biologically meaningful regions (e.g., splice sites), adding some mechanistic insight beyond aggregate metrics.
Ablation isolating the DNA-specific pretraining contribution from the underlying OCR backbone (comparison to vanilla DeepSeek-OCR) is a good practice that isolates the source of improvement.
weaknesses: The central motivating claims (Limitations 1 and 2 in the intro, and the biological justification in Appendix B) are conceptually shaky: the 2D rendering is explicitly acknowledged to encode no biological structure and to be a purely computational reformulation, yet the paper repeatedly frames this as addressing 'sparse, discontinuous genomic semantics' — the actual mechanism of benefit (patch-based tokenization plus a large pretrained multimodal backbone) is not clearly distinguished from simply obtaining a stronger, differently-tokenized representation.

The six 'OCR-inspired genomic primitive' tasks, which are advertised as a key contribution aligning OCR with genomic reasoning, perform poorly in absolute terms in the appendix evaluations (e.g., T6 chromosome classification accuracy of only 6–10%, T4 masked completion Text-EM ~13%, T5 localization Det-Acc collapsing under strict IoU), undermining the claimed close alignment between OCR primitives and genomic reasoning that motivates the framework.

Downstream evaluation is entirely based on frozen-encoder linear/shallow-MLP probing, so the reported gains mainly reflect representation quality of a pretrained vision-language backbone rather than genuinely novel task-specific genomic reasoning; it is unclear how much of the improvement is attributable to the large capacity/pretraining of the underlying DeepSeek-OCR VLM versus the proposed DNA-specific pretraining tasks (the backbone-vs-full-model ablation shows a comparatively modest +5.4% relative gain).

Some controlled comparisons meant to justify the 2D-vs-1D framing use weak or apparently under-tuned 1D baselines (e.g., Transformer-tiny/small achieving only 0.475–0.575 AUROC, seemingly far below typical Transformer capability), raising concerns that the 1D vs 2D comparison may be biased in favor of the proposed approach rather than a fair architectural comparison.

Several benchmarks used for headline claims are very small (RiceWGPB has only 102–130 total samples with 70/10/20 splits), and no error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported anywhere in the main results, making it difficult to assess the statistical robustness of reported improvements, especially for close numbers (e.g., TGW RMSE 2.95 vs 3.06).

Baselines without native long-context support (NT-v2-500M, GENERator-1.2B, Evo-2 via chunking) are evaluated under a chunked/frozen-backbone protocol that may not reflect their intended or best-case usage, potentially disadvantaging them relative to OpticalDNA's tailored pipeline.

The extensive supplementary material, while valuable for reproducibility, also somewhat obscures a clear-eyed treatment of the framework's weaker results (e.g., poor absolute performance on 4/6 of the newly proposed tasks) within the main text, giving an overly optimistic impression of task alignment in the abstract and introduction relative to what the appendices actually show.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem (efficient long-context genomic modeling) and proposes a genuinely creative reformulation—casting DNA sequences as rendered visual documents and reusing an OCR/vision-language pipeline (DeepSeek-OCR) with prompt-conditioned tasks (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion).

Extensive empirical coverage: three benchmark suites (DNALONGBench eQTL, RiceSubBench, RiceWGPB), multiple ablations (token bottleneck, rendering robustness, low-resolution downsampling, cross-species transfer, Grad-CAM interpretability), and a thorough contamination/leakage analysis.
Reasonably strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices specify prompts, conversation formats, rendering procedures, hyperparameter search spaces, and pretraining schedules.

Parameter-efficient adaptation (frozen backbone + small trainable head) is appealing from a practical standpoint, and the method shows consistent gains over the backbone (DeepSeek-OCR) and several sequence-based baselines in the reported settings.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim—that 2D visual rendering better captures 'jump-like dependencies across distant loci' and sparse/discontinuous genomic signals (Fig. 1a)—is not actually substantiated by the method itself: the rendering is a simple left-to-right, top-to-bottom text wrap of the raw 1D sequence, so spatially distant interacting loci are not brought closer in the 2D layout; the biological argument in Appendix B is explicitly walked back to a vague 'computational interface' framing, which reads as a post-hoc rationalization rather than a principled design justification.

The efficiency narrative is inconsistent with the paper's own data: Table S36 shows OpticalDNA has substantially higher FLOPs/base (177.76) than JanusDNA (17.95) and Caduceus (27.27), and comparable-or-worse fine-tuning/inference throughput than several baselines, yet the abstract and main text repeatedly emphasize 'nearly 20× fewer effective tokens' and '985× fewer activated parameters' without foregrounding these countervailing compute-cost numbers in the main text.

Comparisons appear tilted in several places: NT-v2-500M and GENERator-1.2B are evaluated via chunked frozen-backbone linear probes because they 'do not natively support 450 kb inputs,' which handicaps them relative to their intended usage; Evo-2, used prominently as a strong baseline in the rice benchmarks, is conspicuously absent from the main human eQTL comparison (Table 2), the paper's headline result.

The 1D vs. 2D 'controlled comparisons' in Appendix A rely on weak or seemingly undertuned 1D baselines (e.g., a 0.406M-parameter 'Transformer-tiny' scoring only 0.475 AUROC, far below a basic 1D CNN), which undermines confidence that the 2D advantage is not partly an artifact of baseline under-optimization rather than a genuine representational benefit.

Several downstream benchmarks are very small (RiceWGPB has only 102–130 total samples with 10–26 test examples; RiceSubBench group sizes range from 4 to 58 accessions), and no result is reported with multiple seeds, variance, or confidence intervals anywhere in the paper, making the 'state-of-the-art' claims statistically fragile.

The performance gains over the strongest prior baseline (JanusDNA) on the main eQTL benchmark are fairly modest in absolute terms (0.867 vs. 0.840 average AUROC for MLP heads), despite OpticalDNA building on a massively pretrained multi-billion-parameter OCR foundation model (SAM+CLIP+3B MoE decoder); no ablation isolates how much of the gain stems from this powerful general-purpose pretrained visual backbone versus the proposed DNA-specific OCR pretraining tasks, beyond a single comparison against the unmodified DeepSeek-OCR backbone.

The overall framing ('Rethinking Genomic Modeling') is broader than what is actually validated: evaluation is restricted to eQTL classification, splice-site classification under domain shift, and two small whole-genome phenotype regression tasks in rice, rather than the more standard and diverse genomic benchmarks (e.g., GUE, BEND, promoter/enhancer/TF-binding tasks) that would better establish general-purpose utility of the proposed paradigm.

strengths: Highly original reframing of genomic sequence modeling as OCR-style document understanding, introducing a coherent set of six prompt-conditioned tasks (reading, grounding, retrieval, completion) that map naturally onto practical genomic operations (variant localization, subsequence search, imputation).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation across three progressively harder benchmarks (DNALONGBENCH eQTL, RiceSubBench cross-subspecies OOD, RiceWGPB whole-genome phenotype prediction), with consistent gains over strong baselines (JanusDNA, NT-v2, GENERator, Evo-2, LucaOne) while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable/activated parameters.

Unusually thorough appendix addressing typical reviewer concerns proactively: train/test contamination analysis via strict full-sequence and k-mer overlap, rendering/formatting robustness (layout, font, resolution, fragment partitioning), token-bottleneck ablations, cross-species transfer controls, and end-to-end compute/memory/throughput comparisons.

Controlled 1D-vs-2D and matched-token-budget experiments (Appendix A) attempt to isolate the effect of the visual reformulation itself from confounds like backbone capacity or compression ratio, strengthening the causal claim that document-style reorganization of computation helps.

Interpretability analysis (Grad-CAM on multi-page fusion) shows plausible alignment between visual attribution and biologically meaningful splice-site loci, adding qualitative support beyond aggregate metrics.
Clear, detailed documentation of the rendering pipeline, conversation schema, and task protocols (Appendices C–F) that would support reproducibility if code is released.
weaknesses: Core architecture relies on a large pretrained natural-document OCR backbone (DeepSeek-OCR, ~3B decoder) whose priors come from natural-language/document images; the paper does not deeply justify or ablate whether/how much this prior actually transfers to DNA semantics versus simply providing a powerful frozen feature extractor, making the 'activated parameter' efficiency comparisons somewhat misleading since the massive upstream OCR pretraining cost is not counted.

Downstream evaluation is restricted to frozen-backbone linear/MLP probing; it remains unclear how OpticalDNA would compare under full fine-tuning or how robust conclusions are when baselines are evaluated under comparable protocols, especially since several baselines (NT-v2, GENERator) are also forced into a non-native frozen-probe setting for fair comparison, potentially disadvantaging them.

Some of the custom task evaluations reveal weak absolute performance (e.g., T6 chromosome classification accuracy of only 6–10%, T4 masked completion exact-match ~13%), which undercuts the claim that the six OCR-style primitives yield strong 'base-level understanding'; these results are reported honestly but are not well reconciled with the paper's broader narrative of effective genomic reasoning.

The RiceWGPB benchmark has very small sample sizes (test sets of 21 and 26 examples), so RMSE differences between OpticalDNA and baselines (e.g., 2.95 vs 3.06 for Evo-2) may not be statistically meaningful, yet are presented as a clear win.

The 1D vs 2D CNN/Transformer comparisons in Appendix A use comparatively small/under-optimized 1D baselines against well-established, ImageNet-style 2D backbones (TinyNet, MobileNetV3); architecture maturity and transfer-learning advantages of the 2D models could confound the claimed intrinsic benefit of sparse/discontinuous 2D genomic layouts.

No concrete code/data release is demonstrated in the manuscript (placeholder links only), and the dense, highly customized rendering/task pipeline (fonts, line spacing, prompt curricula, truncation schedules) introduces many hyperparameters that could make faithful reproduction difficult without released artifacts.

The conceptual motivation (DNA as a 'document' with 2D layout) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors themselves to be a computational reformulation rather than a biologically grounded one, which is reasonable, but this somewhat weakens the scientific novelty claim beyond 'a compression/tokenization trick wrapped in an OCR interface.'
